progressCard.title: Your retirement goal
progressCard.growth: Your current {current} grows to {projected} by retirement at a cautious {rate} per year — that's {pct}% of the target shown above (before adding any monthly savings). At the expected {expectedRate} it would be {expectedPct}%.
progressCard.netDebt: Your liabilities exceed your assets by {debt}. Your plan starts from {zero}, so paying down that debt comes on top of the monthly savings we calculate.
progressCard.pensionsCoverAll: Your pension income already covers your expected expenses — no portfolio drawdown required.

savingsCard.title: How much to save each month
savingsCard.pensionsCoverAll: Your pensions cover your expected expenses, so you don't need to save toward a retirement portfolio.
savingsCard.onTrack: Based on your current assets and expected growth, you're on track to reach your goal without saving anything extra. Keep it up!
savingsCard.expectedHint: assumes {rate} / yr — a portfolio that doubles roughly every {years, plural, one {# year} other {# years}}
savingsCard.indexed: First month's amount, rising with inflation — to {amount} (expected) by retirement.
savingsCard.flat: A flat nominal amount each month until retirement; inflation makes the later payments worth less.
savingsCard.netDebt: These amounts start from {zero} and don't include paying down your current debt.
savingsCard.mortgageNotProjected: Your home mortgage's full balance of {balance} counts as still owed at retirement and is part of your target: add its rate and repayment in the plan to project it.
savingsCard.mortgageOwedAtRetirement: On top of this, your home mortgage repayments of {payment}/mo continue from your income; the {balance} still owed at retirement is part of your target.
savingsCard.mortgageRepaidBefore: On top of this, your home mortgage repayments of {payment}/mo continue from your income until the loan is repaid.

chart.title: Projected portfolio growth
chart.footnote: Four paths: your expected and conservative returns, each shown with your monthly saving plan and with your current portfolio left to grow on its own. The dashed line is your target.

explainer.trigger: Why these numbers? The 4% rule, explained
explainer.rule: The 4% rule is a simple guideline: each year you can withdraw about 4% of your portfolio without running it down over a long retirement. Flip that around and your portfolio needs to be 25× the yearly amount it has to cover.
explainer.customRate: Your plan uses {rate} instead, so your portfolio needs to be {multiple}× that amount.
explainer.marketReturn: ≈ 7–8% long-run expected market return per year
explainer.inflation: − ~2% inflation, so your money keeps its purchasing power
explainer.buffer: − a buffer to stay safe in bad market years
explainer.result: = about 4% you can spend each year
explainer.inflationHandlingRate: Because the withdrawal rate already accounts for inflation during retirement, we don't add inflation twice. Before retirement we grow your expenses and pensions by {rate} a year and grow each part of your portfolio at its own expected return — keeping everything consistent.
explainer.inflationHandling: Because the withdrawal rate already accounts for inflation during retirement, we don't add inflation twice. Before retirement we grow your expenses and pensions by the inflation rate and grow each part of your portfolio at its own expected return — keeping everything consistent.
explainer.simpleTarget: For your plan, using today's expenses and today's pensions (no inflation) the target would be {target}.
explainer.adjustedTargetRate: Adjusted for {years} of {rate} inflation, the realistic target is {target}.
explainer.adjustedTarget: Adjusted for {years} of inflation, the realistic target is {target}.
explainer.difference: {reason, select, fixedPensionsAndMortgage {The difference is inflation, which your fixed pensions don't keep up with, plus the mortgage still owed when you retire.} fixedPensions {The difference is inflation, which your fixed pensions don't keep up with.} mortgage {The difference is inflation, plus the mortgage still owed when you retire.} other {The difference is inflation.}}
